name: Mars
tagline: A world written in rust.
clues: A dusty horizon stretches ahead. The ground is rocky, and the atmosphere is far too thin to breathe.
Iron minerals in the soil have oxidized, giving this world its distinctive rusty color.
This is the fourth planet from the Sun, home to Olympus Mons and the Perseverance rover.
explanation: Welcome to Mars, the Red Planet. Its rusty color comes from oxidized iron in the soil. Ancient riverbeds and lake deposits show that liquid water once shaped this now cold, dry world. Olympus Mons is the largest volcano in the solar system.
fact: A day here lasts about 24 hours and 39 minutes.
note: A real rover mosaic. Color processing and stitched image boundaries may be visible. The sky and missing polar coverage are reconstructed for spherical viewing.

name: The Moon
tagline: Our closest, quietest neighbor.
clues: The sky is black even in daylight. A gray, cratered landscape lies silent beneath your feet.
There is almost no atmosphere here. Footprints can remain in the dusty surface for a very long time.
You are on Earth's only natural satellite, first visited by humans in 1969.
explanation: You have landed on the Moon. Its surface is covered in powdery regolith and impact craters. With almost no atmosphere, it has extreme swings between day and night temperatures. The Moon is tidally locked, so the same side always faces Earth.
fact: The Moon drifts about 3.8 centimeters farther from Earth each year.
note: An Apollo photographic panorama, adapted to a sphere with reconstructed missing coverage. ¹Distance is the average from Earth, rather than from the Sun.

name: Europa
tagline: An ocean, hidden beneath the ice.
clues: A bright, frozen crust stretches toward a dark horizon. Long fractures cross the icy ground.
Scientists have strong evidence that a salty ocean lies beneath this world's outer ice shell.
You orbit Jupiter. This icy moon is the destination of NASA's Europa Clipper mission.
explanation: This is Europa, one of Jupiter's largest moons. Beneath its fractured ice shell, a global salty ocean may contain more water than all of Earth's oceans combined. Tidal forces from Jupiter help heat its interior. Its ocean makes Europa a compelling place to investigate habitability.
fact: Europa completes an orbit around Jupiter in about 3.5 Earth days.
note: An imagined surface informed by spacecraft observations; no lander has photographed Europa's surface. Jupiter's size and position are illustrative. ²Distance follows its host planet.

name: Titan
tagline: Familiar landscapes. Alien chemistry.
clues: A thick orange haze hangs above dark terrain. Rounded stones rest on a strangely familiar shore.
Rain, rivers, and lakes shape this world, but the liquid is methane and ethane rather than water.
This is Saturn's largest moon, and the only moon in our solar system with a dense atmosphere.
explanation: Welcome to Titan. Saturn's largest moon has a nitrogen-rich atmosphere, dunes, and lakes of liquid methane and ethane. At about minus 179 degrees Celsius, water ice behaves like rock. The Huygens probe landed here in 2005, revealing a landscape shaped by flowing liquid.
fact: Titan is larger than the planet Mercury.
note: An imagined shoreline informed by Cassini-Huygens observations. This is not a Huygens photograph. ²Distance follows its host planet.

name: Venus
tagline: Beauty with a crushing atmosphere.
clues: The rocky landscape is washed in yellow-orange light. A dense sky hides the Sun completely.
The atmosphere is mostly carbon dioxide, and surface pressure is about 90 times Earth's.
You are on the second planet from the Sun, the hottest planet in our solar system.
explanation: This is Venus. A thick carbon dioxide atmosphere traps heat through an extreme greenhouse effect, making it hotter than Mercury. Clouds of sulfuric acid hide its surface. Venus rotates very slowly and in the opposite direction to most planets.
fact: One rotation takes about 243 Earth days, longer than its 225-day year.
note: An imagined surface informed by Venera photographs and radar mapping. Terrain, sky, and lighting are artistic approximations.

name: Black hole
tagline: Where even light takes a detour.
clues: A dark silhouette interrupts the stars. A brilliant band of hot material curves around it.
Gravity bends the light behind this object, distorting the appearance of its accretion disk.
Beyond its event horizon, nothing can escape, not even light. Your spacecraft remains outside.
explanation: You are observing a simulated black hole from outside its event horizon. The bright accretion disk is hot matter orbiting the black hole. Gravity bends light from the far side into view, creating a warped image. The dark central shadow is larger than the event horizon itself.
fact: Black holes are detected by how they affect nearby matter and light.
note: An illustrative view, not an actual spacecraft photograph or a calculated ray-tracing model. No particular black hole or viewing distance is represented.

name: Mercury
tagline: A year on Mercury lasts about 88 Earth days.
credit: NASA/Johns Hopkins University Applied Physics Laboratory/Carnegie Institution of Washington
clues: An ancient rocky surface is crowded with impact craters. There is almost no atmosphere to soften the extremes.
Its heavily cratered landscape includes the enormous Caloris basin. It has no moons.
The smallest planet travels closest to the Sun. MESSENGER mapped it from orbit.
explanation: Mercury is the innermost and smallest planet. With almost no atmosphere, its rocky surface experiences extreme temperature changes. Craters preserve a long record of impacts.
fact: A year on Mercury lasts about 88 Earth days.
note: MESSENGER Explores Mercury - In Color. Resized and JPEG compressed; telescope colors may represent non-visible wavelengths.

name: Jupiter
tagline: Jupiter rotates once in roughly ten hours.
clues: Cloud bands sweep across a giant world with no solid surface to land on.
A vast, long-lived storm swirls through the southern cloud bands.
This is the largest planet, with the Great Red Spot and the moons Io and Europa.
explanation: Jupiter is a gas giant dominated by hydrogen and helium. Its cloud bands and Great Red Spot are part of a turbulent atmosphere, which the Juno mission studies up close.
fact: Jupiter rotates once in roughly ten hours.
note: Jupiter Great Red Spot. Resized and JPEG compressed; telescope colors may represent non-visible wavelengths.

name: Saturn
tagline: Saturn has a lower average density than water.
clues: A pale giant is surrounded by a broad, thin disk of countless small particles.
The bright rings are made largely of water ice. A hexagonal jet stream surrounds its north pole.
The sixth planet is home to Titan and Enceladus and was explored by Cassini.
explanation: Saturn is a hydrogen-rich gas giant whose spectacular rings are mostly ice particles. Cassini explored the planet, rings, and moons for more than a decade.
fact: Saturn has a lower average density than water.
note: The Greatest Saturn Portrait ...Yet. Resized and JPEG compressed; telescope colors may represent non-visible wavelengths.

name: Io
tagline: Some volcanic plumes on Io rise hundreds of kilometers.
clues: Bright deposits and dark volcanic regions mark a rocky satellite.
Tidal flexing heats its interior, powering extraordinary volcanic activity.
This sulfur-rich moon is the innermost of Jupiter’s four large Galilean satellites.
explanation: Io is the most volcanically active world in the solar system. Gravitational interactions with Jupiter and neighboring moons flex its interior, generating heat.
fact: Some volcanic plumes on Io rise hundreds of kilometers.
note: Io Surface Deposits and Volcano. Resized and JPEG compressed; telescope colors may represent non-visible wavelengths.

name: Enceladus
tagline: Its south-polar fractures are nicknamed tiger stripes.
clues: A small, bright icy world appears against the blackness of space.
Jets escape through fractures near its south pole, carrying water from an ocean below.
Cassini sampled the plumes of this moon, whose material helps supply Saturn’s E ring.
explanation: Enceladus hides a global ocean beneath an icy shell. Its south-polar geysers carry water vapor, ice grains, salts, and organic material into space.
fact: Its south-polar fractures are nicknamed tiger stripes.
note: Peaceful Portrait. Resized and JPEG compressed; telescope colors may represent non-visible wavelengths.

name: Ceres
tagline: Ceres was discovered in 1801.
clues: An impact-scarred small world has striking bright deposits inside a crater.
Salts left behind by briny material create the bright areas in Occator crater.
Dawn orbited this dwarf planet, the largest object in the main asteroid belt.
explanation: Ceres is a dwarf planet between Mars and Jupiter. Dawn revealed salts in bright crater deposits, evidence of a complex history involving water.
fact: Ceres was discovered in 1801.
note: Occator Crater and Ceres Brightest Spots. Resized and JPEG compressed; telescope colors may represent non-visible wavelengths.

name: Pluto
tagline: Its bright heart-shaped region is called Tombaugh Regio.
credit: NASA/Johns Hopkins University Applied Physics Laboratory/Southwest Research Institute
clues: Pale plains meet rougher terrain on a very distant icy world.
A vast nitrogen-ice plain forms part of a familiar heart-shaped region.
New Horizons visited this Kuiper Belt dwarf planet in 2015. Its largest moon is Charon.
explanation: Pluto has mountains of water ice, nitrogen glaciers, and a thin atmosphere. The New Horizons flyby revealed a surprisingly active and varied landscape.
fact: Its bright heart-shaped region is called Tombaugh Regio.
note: Frozen Plains in the Heart of Pluto Heart. Resized and JPEG compressed; cropped to remove identifying annotation; telescope colors may represent non-visible wavelengths.

name: Vesta
tagline: Some meteorites on Earth originated on Vesta.
clues: An uneven, rocky body bears an enormous record of impacts.
A giant impact basin dominates its south pole. This body has differentiated layers.
Dawn explored this asteroid before traveling on to Ceres.
explanation: Vesta is a large asteroid with a crust, mantle, and core. Ancient impacts excavated material that sometimes reaches Earth as meteorites.
fact: Some meteorites on Earth originated on Vesta.
note: A Full-Frame View of Vesta. Resized and JPEG compressed; cropped to remove identifying annotation; telescope colors may represent non-visible wavelengths.

name: Bennu
tagline: Bennu’s surface is much more loosely packed than it looks.
clues: Boulders crowd the surface of a small, dark, rocky body.
This rubble pile was the target of a mission that collected loose surface material.
OSIRIS-REx brought samples from this asteroid to Earth in 2023.
explanation: Bennu is a carbon-rich rubble-pile asteroid. OSIRIS-REx collected a sample that helps scientists investigate the early solar system and the chemistry of life’s ingredients.
fact: Bennu’s surface is much more loosely packed than it looks.
note: A Region of Bennu’s Northern Hemisphere Close Up. Resized and JPEG compressed; telescope colors may represent non-visible wavelengths.

name: Eros
tagline: The NEAR spacecraft was not originally designed as a lander.
clues: A rugged rocky landscape covers an elongated small body.
Its shape includes a distinctive saddle region between higher areas.
NEAR Shoemaker orbited this asteroid and landed on it in 2001.
explanation: Eros is an elongated near-Earth asteroid. NEAR Shoemaker mapped it in detail and became the first spacecraft to land on an asteroid.
fact: The NEAR spacecraft was not originally designed as a lander.
note: Back in the Saddle Again. Resized and JPEG compressed; telescope colors may represent non-visible wavelengths.

name: The Sun
tagline: Sunlight takes about eight minutes to reach Earth.
clues: A turbulent, glowing surface sends arches of hot material into space.
Magnetic fields shape prominences and dark sunspots on this nearby star.
This star anchors our solar system and supplies most of Earth’s energy.
explanation: The Sun is a main-sequence star powered by hydrogen fusion in its core. Magnetic activity drives flares, prominences, and changes in the solar wind.
fact: Sunlight takes about eight minutes to reach Earth.
note: Churning Prominence. Resized and JPEG compressed; telescope colors may represent non-visible wavelengths.

name: White dwarf
tagline: A white dwarf can pack a star’s worth of mass into an Earth-sized volume.
clues: A compact bright object is surrounded by disrupted material in this artist’s concept.
This remnant no longer sustains ordinary hydrogen fusion in its core.
A Sun-like star leaves behind this dense, roughly Earth-sized core after shedding its outer layers.
explanation: A white dwarf is a dense stellar remnant. The illustration shows debris around G29-38, a white dwarf whose surrounding dust was studied with Spitzer.
fact: A white dwarf can pack a star’s worth of mass into an Earth-sized volume.
note: Comet Bites the Dust Around Dead Star  Artist Concept. Resized and JPEG compressed; telescope colors may represent non-visible wavelengths.

name: Red supergiant
tagline: Betelgeuse is in the constellation Orion.
clues: A luminous star is surrounded by an extended envelope of expelled material.
Massive stars can swell and cool at the surface late in their lives.
Betelgeuse, shown here in infrared, is a famous example of this enormous red stellar type.
explanation: Red supergiants are evolved massive stars with very large, cool outer layers. This infrared view shows Betelgeuse and surrounding material, rather than a resolved visible-light surface.
fact: Betelgeuse is in the constellation Orion.
note: Betelgeuse Enigmatic Environment. Resized and JPEG compressed; telescope colors may represent non-visible wavelengths.

name: Protostar
tagline: Infrared telescopes can see forming stars hidden by dust.
credit: NASA/ESA/JPL-Caltech/STScI/NOAO/University of Arizona/ Max Planck Institute for Astronomy/University of Massachusetts, Amherst
clues: A young light source is still surrounded by the material from which it is forming.
Gas collapses under gravity; disks and outflows can accompany this early stage.
This infant object has not yet settled into stable main-sequence hydrogen fusion.
explanation: A protostar forms as a cloud of gas and dust collapses. Material accretes onto the growing object before it reaches the main sequence. This image shows the young system LRLL 54361.
fact: Infrared telescopes can see forming stars hidden by dust.
note: Protostar LRLL 54361. Resized and JPEG compressed; cropped to remove identifying annotation; telescope colors may represent non-visible wavelengths.

name: Red dwarf
tagline: Red dwarfs are the most common type of star in the Milky Way.
clues: A small, cool star throws off a powerful flare in this illustration.
These low-mass stars burn their hydrogen slowly and can remain active for very long periods.
Proxima Centauri belongs to this common, faint, red main-sequence stellar class.
explanation: Red dwarfs are small, relatively cool main-sequence stars. Although dim, some produce intense flares. This image is an artist’s illustration of a flaring red dwarf.
fact: Red dwarfs are the most common type of star in the Milky Way.
note: Flaring Red Dwarf Star (Illustration). Resized and JPEG compressed; telescope colors may represent non-visible wavelengths.

name: 1P/Halley
tagline: Halley is associated with the Orionid and Eta Aquariid meteor showers.
clues: A dark, irregular icy nucleus releases material as it warms.
This famous traveler returns to the inner solar system roughly every 76 years.
Its predicted return confirmed Edmond Halley’s orbital calculations. Giotto visited it in 1986.
explanation: Halley is a periodic comet whose icy nucleus sheds gas and dust near the Sun. The Giotto spacecraft revealed its dark surface during the 1986 encounter.
fact: Halley is associated with the Orionid and Eta Aquariid meteor showers.
note: Comet Halley. Resized and JPEG compressed; telescope colors may represent non-visible wavelengths.

name: 67P/Churyumov–Gerasimenko
tagline: Philae was the first spacecraft to land on a comet.
credit: Copyright: ESA/Rosetta/MPS for OSIRIS Team MPS/UPD/LAM/IAA/SSO/INTA/UPM/DASP/IDA
clues: Two irregular lobes join at a narrow neck on this icy body.
A spacecraft orbited it while a small lander touched down on its surface.
ESA’s Rosetta and the Philae lander explored this comet in 2014.
explanation: Comet 67P has two joined lobes and an active surface. Rosetta followed it around the Sun, observing how solar heating drives jets of gas and dust.
fact: Philae was the first spacecraft to land on a comet.
note: Comet 67P from 1,200 Miles Away. Resized and JPEG compressed; telescope colors may represent non-visible wavelengths.

name: 9P/Tempel 1
tagline: The Stardust-NExT mission revisited Tempel 1 in 2011.
clues: A rough, irregular nucleus is viewed close up by a spacecraft.
A deliberate impact exposed material from beneath its surface.
Deep Impact sent an impactor into this comet on July 4, 2005.
explanation: Tempel 1 was the target of NASA’s Deep Impact experiment. The impact and subsequent observations helped reveal the physical properties of cometary material.
fact: The Stardust-NExT mission revisited Tempel 1 in 2011.
note: Tempel 1 Nucleus. Resized and JPEG compressed; telescope colors may represent non-visible wavelengths.

name: 81P/Wild 2
tagline: A close encounter with Jupiter changed Wild 2’s orbit in 1974.
clues: An irregular nucleus has deep depressions and rugged relief.
A passing spacecraft collected dust from its coma in aerogel.
Stardust returned samples from this comet to Earth in 2006.
explanation: Wild 2 was visited by Stardust, which collected tiny particles from its coma. Those samples give laboratories direct evidence about material from the early solar system.
fact: A close encounter with Jupiter changed Wild 2’s orbit in 1974.
note: Comet Wild 2 Up Close and Personal. Resized and JPEG compressed; telescope colors may represent non-visible wavelengths.

name: 103P/Hartley 2
tagline: Hartley 2 has a distinctive peanut-like shape.
clues: A small nucleus has two ends connected by a smoother waist.
Jets driven by carbon dioxide helped eject chunks of ice from this hyperactive body.
The EPOXI mission flew past this comet in 2010.
explanation: Hartley 2 is a small, active comet explored by EPOXI. Its uneven activity and smooth waist reveal how material moves and escapes from a cometary nucleus.
fact: Hartley 2 has a distinctive peanut-like shape.
note: Almost There at Comet Hartley 2. Resized and JPEG compressed; telescope colors may represent non-visible wavelengths.

name: Pulsar
tagline: Some pulsars spin hundreds of times per second.
clues: Rings and a jet surround a tiny, energetic central object in an X-ray image.
A rapidly spinning neutron star sends beams of radiation across space.
When those beams sweep past Earth, this stellar remnant appears to pulse like a lighthouse.
explanation: A pulsar is a rotating neutron star with beams of radiation. This Chandra image shows the Crab pulsar’s energetic surroundings, including rings and a jet.
fact: Some pulsars spin hundreds of times per second.
note: History of Chandra X-Ray Observatory. Resized and JPEG compressed; telescope colors may represent non-visible wavelengths.

name: Supernova remnant
tagline: Supernova explosions help distribute elements needed for rocky planets.
clues: A shell of glowing debris spreads through space in this composite image.
An exploded star sent shock waves outward and enriched its surroundings with heavy elements.
Cassiopeia A is a famous example of the expanding remnant left after a massive star’s supernova.
explanation: Supernova remnants contain the expanding debris and shock waves of stellar explosions. Cassiopeia A is observed at many wavelengths to trace different elements and energies.
fact: Supernova explosions help distribute elements needed for rocky planets.
note: Cassiopeia A: Death Becomes Her. Resized and JPEG compressed; telescope colors may represent non-visible wavelengths.

name: Planetary nebula
type: Gas shed by an aging star
tagline: The misleading name comes from their planet-like appearance in early telescopes.
clues: A glowing shell surrounds a fading stellar core.
A lower-mass star has shed its outer layers, which are lit by the exposed hot remnant.
Despite the name, this object is unrelated to planets. The Helix is a well-known example.
explanation: A planetary nebula forms when an aging lower-mass star loses its outer layers. Ultraviolet light from the exposed hot core makes the expanding gas glow.
fact: The misleading name comes from their planet-like appearance in early telescopes.
note: Planetary Nebula NGC 7293 also Known as the Helix Nebula. Resized and JPEG compressed; telescope colors may represent non-visible wavelengths.
scale: Gas shed by an aging star

name: Gravitational lens
tagline: Astronomers use gravitational lenses as natural telescopes.
clues: Distant light appears stretched into curved arcs around foreground objects.
A massive foreground object bends and magnifies light arriving from behind it.
This effect, predicted by general relativity, can produce an Einstein ring.
explanation: Gravitational lensing occurs when mass curves the path of light. This Hubble image of a galaxy cluster shows curved images of more distant galaxies.
fact: Astronomers use gravitational lenses as natural telescopes.
note: Hubble Sees A Smiling Lens. Resized and JPEG compressed; telescope colors may represent non-visible wavelengths.

name: Andromeda
tagline: Andromeda lies about 2.5 million light-years away.
clues: A large tilted disk has a bright center and long dusty lanes.
This major spiral belongs to the Local Group alongside our own galaxy.
Also called M31, it is the nearest large spiral galaxy to the Milky Way.
explanation: Andromeda is a large spiral galaxy in the Local Group. Its inclined disk contains star-forming regions, dust lanes, and a bright central bulge.
fact: Andromeda lies about 2.5 million light-years away.
note: Andromeda Galaxy. Resized and JPEG compressed; telescope colors may represent non-visible wavelengths.

name: Whirlpool
tagline: M51 is a favorite target for studying spiral structure.
credit: NASA and The Hubble Heritage Team STScI/AURA Acknowledgement: N. Scoville Caltech and T. Rector NOAO
clues: Graceful spiral arms curl around a bright galactic center.
A smaller companion interacts with the main spiral, helping shape its structure.
This face-on spiral pair is cataloged as M51.
explanation: The Whirlpool Galaxy is a spiral interacting with a smaller companion. Its prominent arms trace dust, gas, and regions where young stars are forming.
fact: M51 is a favorite target for studying spiral structure.
note: Whirlpool Galaxy. Resized and JPEG compressed; telescope colors may represent non-visible wavelengths.

name: Sombrero
tagline: Its central region hosts a supermassive black hole.
clues: A bright central bulge rises above a thin, dark band of dust.
Viewed nearly edge-on, its silhouette resembles a broad-brimmed hat.
This galaxy is cataloged as M104 and named for its hat-like appearance.
explanation: The Sombrero Galaxy has a prominent central bulge and a striking dust lane. Its near-edge-on orientation creates its characteristic silhouette.
fact: Its central region hosts a supermassive black hole.
note: Hubble Spies Spectacular Sombrero. Resized and JPEG compressed; telescope colors may represent non-visible wavelengths.

name: Triangulum
tagline: M33 contains the enormous star-forming region NGC 604.
clues: A loosely wound spiral contains many bright regions of star formation.
This relatively small Local Group spiral lacks a large central bulge.
Cataloged as M33, it takes its name from the constellation of the Triangle.
explanation: The Triangulum Galaxy is a Local Group spiral with extensive star-forming regions. Multiwavelength observations reveal its gas, dust, and young stellar populations.
fact: M33 contains the enormous star-forming region NGC 604.
note: M33: A Close Neighbor Reveals its True Size and Splendor 3-color composite. Resized and JPEG compressed; telescope colors may represent non-visible wavelengths.

name: Large Magellanic Cloud
type: Satellite galaxy of the Milky Way
tagline: It is visible to the unaided eye from much of the Southern Hemisphere.
clues: A patchy, irregular island of stars and dust glows in infrared light.
It is a nearby satellite of our galaxy, rich in star-forming regions.
The Tarantula Nebula lies in this larger of the two famous Magellanic Clouds.
explanation: The Large Magellanic Cloud is a nearby satellite galaxy of the Milky Way. Infrared views reveal dust and stellar populations throughout its irregular structure.
fact: It is visible to the unaided eye from much of the Southern Hemisphere.
note: Our Chaotic Neighbor. Resized and JPEG compressed; telescope colors may represent non-visible wavelengths.
scale: Satellite galaxy of the Milky Way
